newsitem.title: UK: Tunnel fire proves stringent test for security.
newsitem.headline: Tunnel fire proves stringent test for security.

text.p: Channel Tunnel security systems, designed to counter earthquakes, guerrilla bombs and rabid dogs, underwent their most stringent test on Tuesday after a fire on a truck blanketed terrified passengers in toxic smoke.

Truck drivers caught up in a nightmare scenario for the undersea link between Britain and France described having to lie on the floor of the train with pillows and coats over their mouths as thick smoke poured into their carriage.
Two people were seriously affected by smoke inhalation and another six were treated briefly in hospital.
But the remaining 26 were led to safety by French and British rescue services, following what tunnel operators Eurotunnel said was a well-practised emergency drill.
"We have a bi-national emergency plan which we had followed exactly and worked exactly as we anticipated," said Clive Durrant, director of safety for Eurotunnel.
"The operation was led by the French although 100 fire officers from Kent have been involved in containing the incident," he told reporters.
Operators Eurotunnel have always insisted that it is "at least twenty times safer travelling through the tunnel than when travelling by conventional railways".
During the meticulous planning of the 51-km (32-mile) tunnel, opened two years ago, each step was scrutinised by an Anglo-French intergovernmental commission.
Fears that Irish republican guerrillas might use the tunnel to stage a spectacular bomb attack topped the list of concerns.

The tunnel was built to withstand the worst earthquake to have hit southern England in the last millennium and safety systems were designed also to guard against disasters such as fire and even rabid dogs crossing from France into Britain. A central service shaft runs between the two main rail tunnels, allowing rescue services access through entrances every 50 metres.

The service tunnel is also the main means of evacuation, allowing passengers to be treated for injuries there before being led to safety either by walking or boarding a train in the adjoining rail tunnel.

Shuttle trains are fireproof and have fire detection systems and a range of firefighting equipment on board. A freshwater main runs the length of the tunnel and is used by firefighters to douse flames.
Closed circuit television cameras monitor the interior of all shuttle wagons throughout the journey and there is a halon gas fire suppression system.

Cars are driven into fully-enclosed wagons and passengers stay in their vehicles for the 35 minute undersea journey. But trucks drive onto a semi-open wagon and drivers leave their vehicles to gather with colleagues in a passenger cab.
Huge fans at either end of the tunnel control air flow and can be controlled to push smoke and fumes away from passengers.
Drivers caught up in Monday's fire described how smoke from the burning truck billowed towards them from the semi-open wagon, complicating evacuation.
"We realised we couldn't get out because the smoke outside was worse than the smoke inside. We had to stay in the cabin until the rescue services came," said British driver Jeremy Waghorn.
The drivers said staff and firefighters had done a good job but some criticised a lack of oxygen equipment on the train.
"I was breathing intoxicating smoke and I'd got nothing to help me, only a tissue," said Briton Ian Edwards.

"It was like being in a tomb," Brian Shilton told reporters. "Everybody was on the floor and coughing and throwing up and really choking. But not one single person aboard the club car panicked. Everybody was calm."
